panels:
Vertical scaling is underrated: a single modern server can have 192+ cores and several terabytes of RAM, and one well-tuned PostgreSQL box serves a surprising number of companies. It needs no code changes, keeps transactions local and avoids distributed-systems bugs. Its limits are a hard hardware ceiling, cost that rises faster than linearly at the top end, downtime during resizes, and a single failure domain.

Horizontal scaling adds commodity nodes and gives fault tolerance through redundancy, but it pushes complexity into coordination: shared state, data partitioning, consistent configuration and partial failures. Interviewers like the nuance that stateless tiers (web, API) scale out easily, while stateful tiers (databases, caches) are where horizontal scaling gets hard. A common real answer is both: scale the database up as far as is sensible, scale the app tier out.

Stateless does not mean the system has no state; it means a request carries or fetches everything it needs, so no server holds data that a later request depends on. Typical moves: sessions in Redis or in signed, short-lived tokens; uploads in object storage; locks and counters in a shared store; scheduled jobs coordinated with leader election instead of 'run on server 1'.

JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) avoid a session lookup but are hard to revoke before expiry, so keep them short-lived (minutes) with refresh tokens, or keep a small deny-list. Local in-process caches are acceptable as long as losing them only costs performance, not correctness. The payoff is operational: autoscaling, rolling deploys and replacing unhealthy instances become routine because any instance can be killed at any time without losing user data.

An L4 balancer works on TCP/UDP connections: it picks a backend when a connection opens and forwards packets, often via NAT or direct server return, handling millions of connections with tiny overhead. Because it never parses HTTP, it cannot route by path, and with long-lived connections (HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets) it balances connections rather than requests, which can leave load badly skewed.

An L7 balancer (reverse proxy such as Envoy, NGINX, HAProxy or a cloud ALB) terminates TLS, parses requests, and can route by host, path or header, rewrite headers, add retries, do canary splits and balance each gRPC request individually. The cost is CPU per request and a component that sees plaintext traffic. Large sites often chain them: anycast or DNS -> L4 tier -> L7 proxy tier -> services.

Round robin assumes equal servers and equal requests; it is fine for uniform, short requests. Least connections (or least outstanding requests) adapts to uneven request cost and slow backends. A strong practical option is 'power of two choices': pick two servers at random and send to the less loaded one, which gets most of the benefit of global least-load with almost no coordination.

Consistent hashing places servers (often 100-200 virtual nodes each) and keys on a ring; a key goes to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/N of keys, versus nearly all keys with hash % N. Use it when affinity matters, such as cache servers or sharded state. Variants include rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing and bounded-load consistent hashing, which caps how overloaded any one node can get.

Active health checks probe an endpoint on a schedule; passive checks (outlier detection) watch real traffic and eject hosts that return too many 5xx errors or time out. Use thresholds with hysteresis (for example 3 fails out, 2 passes in) so a host does not flap in and out.

Kubernetes makes the distinction sharp: a failing liveness probe restarts the container, a failing readiness probe only removes it from Service endpoints. A classic outage pattern is a deep health check that also verifies the database: when the database blips, every instance fails health checks at once and the balancer has nothing left to route to. Keep liveness shallow, make readiness reflect only what the instance itself controls, and configure 'fail open' (route to all) if every backend looks unhealthy at the same time.

Interviewers care about the method, not precision: state assumptions, round aggressively, and keep units straight. Useful anchors: 1 day = 86,400 s, roughly 10^5; 1M requests/day is about 12 req/s; peak is often 2-5x the average. Per-node capacity depends heavily on the workload: a simple cached read might reach 10,000+ req/s per core-heavy node, while a request doing database work might manage hundreds.

Size for N+1 or N+2 so you survive losing a node (or a whole availability zone: with 3 zones, each must carry 50% of peak if one fails) and keep utilization near 60-70% for headroom. Also estimate bandwidth (requests x response size) and storage (records x size x retention x replication factor). Finish by naming which resource limits you first: CPU, memory, connections, or the database.

Latency and throughput are linked by Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency. At 2,000 req/s and 50 ms average latency, about 100 requests are in flight; if latency doubles, you need twice the concurrency (threads, connections) to keep the same throughput. As utilization approaches 100%, queueing makes latency rise sharply, which is why systems are run with headroom.

Tail latency dominates user experience at scale: if a page fans out to 100 backends and each has a 1% chance of a slow response, about 63% of page loads hit at least one slow call. Mitigations include hedged requests (send a backup request after the p95 time), timeouts, and reducing fan-out. Memorize orders of magnitude, not exact numbers: memory is nanoseconds, SSD is tens to hundreds of microseconds, network within a datacenter is around half a millisecond, and cross-continent is around 100-150 ms.

Sticky sessions (session affinity) pin a user to one server, which defeats even spreading, concentrates load from heavy users, and loses sessions when that server dies; prefer external session stores. The balancer itself must be redundant: an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP, DNS with multiple addresses, or a managed cloud balancer that is distributed internally.

Scaling the stateless tier often just moves the bottleneck: more app servers open more database connections, and connection limits are hit before CPU, so use connection pooling (PgBouncer or a built-in pool). Retries at the balancer can multiply load during an incident, so cap them with retry budgets. Answer to the check: least connections accounts for requests still running, so a server busy with a long request receives fewer new ones, while round robin keeps dealing work to it regardless.
swe-system-design-01.further: Next, study autoscaling policies (target tracking on CPU or requests per second, and why scaling on queue depth reacts faster), global traffic management (GeoDNS, anycast, multi-region failover), and the 'power of two choices' result for load balancing. Read about tail latency in 'The Tail at Scale' and about connection pooling for databases. Service meshes such as Envoy-based meshes move L7 balancing, retries and health checking into sidecars. Finally, practice capacity estimates until converting daily volumes into requests per second, bandwidth and storage feels automatic.

panels:
A cache only helps if the access pattern is skewed and repeated: many real workloads follow a power law where a small fraction of keys gets most reads. The effective latency is roughly hit_ratio x cache_latency + miss_ratio x (cache_latency + db_latency). Going from a 90% to a 99% hit ratio cuts database reads by 10x, which is why the last few percent of hit ratio matter more than they look.

Caching also trades correctness for speed: every cache is a second copy that can be stale, and it adds a failure mode in which the cache disappears and the database suddenly receives the full load (cold-start or failover). Before adding one, check whether a missing index, a better query, or a read replica solves the problem more simply. Cache what is expensive to compute and read far more often than it changes.

Browser caching is controlled by HTTP headers: Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable for fingerprinted static assets (app.3f9a.js), no-cache (revalidate each time using ETag or Last-Modified, getting a cheap 304 Not Modified) for HTML, and private versus public to keep personalized responses out of shared caches. CDNs honor s-maxage and support stale-while-revalidate and purge APIs, and they shield your origin server from traffic spikes.

Application caches come in two flavors: in-process (fastest, no network hop, but duplicated per instance and inconsistent between instances) and distributed (Redis, Memcached: shared, about 0.2-1 ms per round trip). Many systems use both, with a small local LRU in front of Redis. The database buffer pool (PostgreSQL shared_buffers, InnoDB buffer pool) plus the OS page cache already caches hot pages, so a 'slow database' is often an under-provisioned memory problem.

Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the default: only requested data gets cached and the cache can fail without breaking correctness, but the first request for each key pays the full miss and invalidation is the application's job. Read-through is the same idea with the cache library doing the loading.

Write-through updates the cache on every write, so reads are fresh, but writes pay both latencies and the cache fills with data that may never be read. Write-back (write-behind) acknowledges after the cache write and flushes asynchronously, often batching writes, which is great for write-heavy counters but risks losing acknowledged data and needs a durable or replicated cache. A related option is write-around: write only to the database and let reads populate the cache. Choose per data type rather than per system.

The example uses redis-py: r.get returns bytes or None, and set with ex=300 stores the value with a 300-second expiry in one atomic command. Serialize objects (JSON or MessagePack) and namespace keys (service:entity:id) so they can be scanned and purged by prefix.

The update order matters. 'Write DB, then delete key' still has a rare race: a reader misses, loads the old row, the writer commits and deletes, then the reader writes the old value back. The TTL bounds the damage; stricter setups delete again after a short delay or drive invalidation from the database change stream (change data capture). Avoid 'delete key, then write DB', because a reader can repopulate the old value in between. Interviewers often ask exactly this ordering question.

TTLs bound staleness and also clean up keys nobody will ask for again. Choose them per data type: seconds for prices or stock levels, hours for profile data, a year for content-addressed assets. Redis expires keys lazily on access plus by sampling in the background, so expired keys may use memory briefly.

When memory is full, the eviction policy decides. Redis offers noeviction (writes fail), allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-* variants that only evict keys that have a TTL, and random variants. Its LRU and LFU are approximations based on sampling, not exact lists. LRU suits recency-driven workloads; LFU resists one-off scans that would otherwise flush popular keys. Monitor the eviction count and hit ratio together: frequent evictions with a falling hit ratio mean the working set no longer fits.

Invalidation is hard because the cache and the database cannot be updated atomically, and many keys can depend on one row (a user's name appears in their profile, every comment and many feed pages). Approaches, roughly from simple to robust: TTL only; delete on write; versioned or generational keys, where you bump a version number so old keys simply stop being read; and event-driven invalidation from the database's change log, which catches writes from every code path, including scripts and migrations.

Deleting is safer than updating because concurrent updates can be applied out of order, leaving the older value cached indefinitely. For derived data such as feeds, it is often cheaper to tolerate brief staleness than to track every dependency. Always ask: how stale can this be before a user notices, or before it becomes a correctness bug?

A stampede (thundering herd or dogpile) happens when a popular key expires or the cache restarts. Defenses: single-flight or request coalescing, where one caller recomputes under a short-lived lock (SET key:lock NX EX 10) and others wait or receive the stale value; stale-while-revalidate, which serves the old value while a background refresh runs; probabilistic early expiration, where each reader refreshes slightly early with growing probability; and TTL jitter (for example 300 s plus or minus 10%) so keys loaded together do not expire together.

Cache penetration is repeated lookups for keys that do not exist, often from bots, and each one reaches the database; cache the 'not found' result with a short TTL or put a Bloom filter in front. Cache avalanche is many keys expiring at once or the whole cache failing; plan for a cold cache with warm-up and rate limits on the database.
swe-system-design-02.further: Go deeper with HTTP caching semantics (RFC 9111: Cache-Control, ETag, Vary), CDN features such as tiered caching, origin shield and surrogate keys for targeted purges, and Redis internals (persistence with RDB and AOF, replication, Redis Cluster hash slots). Read about cache consistency at scale, for example lease-based invalidation in large Memcached deployments, and about change data capture tools that invalidate caches from database logs. Also learn admission policies such as TinyLFU, which decide whether a new item deserves to enter the cache at all.

panels:
The real decision is about access patterns and guarantees, not fashion. Relational databases give declarative queries, joins, constraints (foreign keys, unique, check) and multi-row ACID transactions, and modern ones scale further than people assume: read replicas, partitioning, and JSONB columns for semi-structured data cover many 'we need NoSQL' cases.

NoSQL systems usually trade some of that for a specific strength: horizontal write scaling, predictable single-digit-millisecond lookups by key, flexible schemas, or native graph traversal. Many now offer transactions too (MongoDB multi-document, DynamoDB TransactWriteItems), so 'NoSQL means no transactions' is outdated. Distributed SQL databases (Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB) combine SQL with horizontal scaling at the cost of higher write latency from consensus. Interview tip: justify the choice from query shapes, consistency needs and scale, and admit that schema-on-read still means a schema, just enforced in application code.

Document stores keep a whole aggregate (an order with its line items) together, so one read fetches it; they struggle with many-to-many relations and cross-document joins. Key-value stores are the simplest and fastest model; DynamoDB adds a sort key, so a partition key plus sort key supports range queries inside one partition, which enables 'single-table design' where you model data around known queries.

Wide-column stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable, HBase) partition by key and store rows sorted by a clustering key, with very high write throughput thanks to log-structured merge trees (LSM trees); you design one table per query. Graph databases store adjacency directly, so multi-hop traversals ('friends of friends who bought X') do not need repeated joins. Also worth knowing: search engines (inverted indexes), time-series databases, and vector databases for similarity search.

A B+ tree (the variant nearly all databases use) has high fan-out, often hundreds of keys per 8-16 KB page, so a table with a billion rows needs only 3-4 levels, and the top levels stay in memory. Leaves are linked, so range scans and ORDER BY on the indexed columns are cheap.

The leftmost-prefix rule for composite indexes: (a, b) is sorted by a, then by b within each a, so it serves equality on a, equality on a plus a range on b, and ordering by b within a fixed a. Put equality columns before range columns. A covering index includes every column the query needs, enabling an index-only scan with no table lookup. Every index slows inserts and updates and consumes memory, so remove unused ones. Other index types: hash, GIN (full-text, JSONB), GiST and BRIN for huge, naturally ordered tables.

EXPLAIN shows the planner's chosen plan with estimated costs; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports real row counts and timings per node (so wrap writes in a transaction you roll back). Read plans inside out: the deepest nodes run first. Signals to look for are Seq Scan on large tables with selective filters, estimated rows far from actual rows (stale statistics, so run ANALYZE), nested loops over large inputs, and sorts that spill to disk.

The planner may still choose a sequential scan when a filter matches a large fraction of the table, because random index lookups cost more than reading sequentially. In PostgreSQL, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking writes on a busy production table. The numbers on the page (2 s versus 1 ms) are typical for a selective lookup on a table with about 10M rows: O(n) page reads versus 3-4 page reads plus the row fetch.

Atomicity is implemented with undo information or multi-version rows, so a failed transaction leaves no partial effects. Durability comes from the write-ahead log (WAL): changes are appended to the log and flushed (fsync) before the commit is acknowledged, and data pages are written later; after a crash the log is replayed. Group commit batches fsyncs to keep throughput high.

The C in ACID is partly the application's job: the database enforces declared constraints, but business invariants like 'balance never negative' must be expressed as constraints or enforced inside transactions. For the transfer example, use a single transaction with conditional updates (UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 50) and check the affected row count; this avoids the read-then-write race. Durability guarantees also depend on configuration, such as synchronous_commit and replication settings.

Anomalies to know: dirty read (seeing uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (a row changes between two reads), phantom (a re-run range query returns new rows), lost update (two read-modify-write cycles overwrite each other) and write skew (two transactions each check an invariant, then write different rows, breaking it together; the classic case is two on-call doctors both going off call).

Implementations differ from the SQL standard. PostgreSQL's repeatable read is snapshot isolation, which prevents phantoms but allows write skew; its serializable level (SSI) detects dangerous patterns and aborts one transaction, so applications must retry on serialization failures. MySQL InnoDB defaults to repeatable read and uses gap locks. Oracle and PostgreSQL default to read committed. Practical tools: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for pessimistic locking, or a version column for optimistic concurrency control.

Normal forms remove redundancy: 1NF has atomic values, 2NF and 3NF remove columns that depend on only part of the key or on other non-key columns, so each fact lives in exactly one place. That prevents update anomalies, where changing an author's name means updating thousands of rows and missing some.

Denormalization deliberately duplicates data to avoid joins or expensive aggregations on hot read paths: counters (comment_count), embedded snapshots (the price at time of order, which is a correct historical fact, not merely a copy), materialized views, and read models built from events (as in CQRS, command query responsibility segregation). The cost is keeping copies in sync through triggers, application logic or asynchronous jobs, with eventual consistency. In NoSQL stores denormalization is the default, because there are no joins. Measure first: a well-indexed join is often fast enough.

N+1 queries usually come from ORM lazy loading; fix them with eager loading (a JOIN, or a second query using WHERE id IN (...)), and find them with query logs or tracing. SELECT * fetches unneeded columns, prevents index-only scans and breaks when the schema changes. Low-selectivity indexes (a boolean, or status with three values) rarely help unless the queried value is rare, where a partial index (WHERE status = 'failed') works well.

Other classics: missing indexes on foreign keys (slow joins and cascading deletes), functions on indexed columns (WHERE lower(email) = ... needs an expression index), long transactions that hold locks and block cleanup of old row versions, and deep OFFSET pagination. Answer to the check: an index on (a, b) is ordered by a first, so rows with b = 5 are scattered across every a value; the database would have to scan the whole index.
swe-system-design-03.further: Next topics: storage engines (B-trees versus LSM trees and their read, write and space amplification), multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) and vacuuming, query planning and statistics, and connection pooling. 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications' covers data models, storage and transactions in depth. Practice reading EXPLAIN plans on a real PostgreSQL instance, and learn about online schema migrations (expand and contract), partitioning large tables, and NewSQL systems that offer serializable transactions across regions using consensus and synchronized clocks.

panels:
Replication copies the same data, so it improves read capacity and survives node failures, but every replica still stores everything and every write must reach every replica, so it does not scale writes or storage. Sharding splits the data, so each node stores and writes only its slice, but queries that span shards become scatter-gather and cross-shard transactions get expensive.

Production systems combine them: a key maps to a shard, and each shard is a replica set (for example one leader and two followers spread across three availability zones). Replicating 3x across zones is the common default because it survives losing one zone while keeping a majority. Before sharding, exhaust simpler options: vertical scaling, read replicas, caching and archiving cold data, because sharding is hard to undo and changes how every query is written.

Followers apply the leader's change stream: physical WAL shipping (PostgreSQL streaming replication) or a logical row-based log (MySQL binlog). Synchronous replication waits for at least one follower to confirm before acknowledging the commit; making every follower synchronous means one slow node stalls all writes, so a common setup is semi-synchronous: one sync follower, the rest async.

Failover is the hard part: detecting that the leader is dead (timeouts that are too short cause false failovers), promoting the most up-to-date follower, and fencing the old leader so that two leaders never accept writes at once (split brain). With async replication, writes acknowledged by the old leader but not yet replicated are lost on failover. Consensus-based systems (Raft, Paxos, as in etcd, Spanner or CockroachDB) commit a write once a majority has it, so failover loses nothing that was acknowledged.

Multi-leader setups suit multi-region writes, offline-capable clients and collaborative editing, but concurrent writes to the same item conflict. Last-write-wins (LWW) is simple but silently drops data and depends on clocks; better options are application-level merges, version vectors to detect true concurrency, or CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types, such as counters, sets and sequences) that merge automatically and deterministically.

Leaderless systems (Dynamo-style: Cassandra, Riak, ScyllaDB) send each write to N replicas and consider it successful after W acknowledgements; reads query R replicas and take the newest version. With W + R > N (for example N = 3, W = 2, R = 2), read and write sets overlap. Repair mechanisms are read repair, hinted handoff and anti-entropy using Merkle trees. Even with quorums, edge cases such as sloppy quorums and concurrent writes mean you do not get linearizability for free.

Lag is normally milliseconds but can grow to minutes under heavy writes, long-running queries on replicas, or network trouble, so monitor it (bytes or seconds behind) and pull lagging replicas out of rotation. Read-your-writes options: route a user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write; remember the log position (LSN) of the user's last write and only read from replicas that have caught up to it; or read user-owned data (their own profile) from the leader and everything else from replicas.

Related anomalies: monotonic reads (a user hits a fresh replica, then a staler one, and sees time go backwards; fix by pinning a user to one replica) and consistent prefix reads (seeing an answer before its question when partitions replicate independently). Mobile and multi-device users complicate this because the 'same user' arrives through different sessions.

Range sharding keeps keys sorted, so range scans and ordered pagination hit few shards and shards can split automatically when they grow (Bigtable, HBase, and CockroachDB ranges). Its risk is skew from sequential keys. Hash sharding spreads load evenly but destroys ordering. hash % N is the worst variant for growth: changing N moves almost every key. Better: a fixed large number of logical shards (for example 1,024) mapped onto physical nodes, so rebalancing moves whole logical shards (Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots), or consistent hashing.

Choose the shard key so that the most common queries hit a single shard: tenant_id for multi-tenant SaaS keeps each customer's data together. Secondary indexes are either local (each shard indexes its own data, so queries scatter to all shards) or global (partitioned by the indexed value, so writes touch several shards). Directory-based sharding (a lookup service) gives full flexibility at the cost of an extra hop.

Skew comes from popular keys (a celebrity's posts, a viral product), sequential keys (timestamps, auto-increment IDs) and uneven tenants (one enterprise customer larger than all the others). Hashing alone does not fix a single hot key, because every request for that key still lands on one shard.

Mitigations: key salting, where you append a suffix 0-9 when writing and fan out reads across the ten sub-keys, trading read cost for write spread; caching hot reads close to the edge; splitting or isolating heavy tenants onto dedicated shards; using write-optimized structures for counters (sharded counters aggregated periodically); and choosing IDs that do not concentrate writes (UUIDv7 is time-ordered and still hot with range sharding, while random UUIDv4 spreads writes but hurts index locality). Detect skew with per-shard metrics; averages across shards hide it completely.

CAP is narrower than it sounds: C means linearizability, A means every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response, and the choice only applies while a partition is happening. Since partitions cannot be ruled out, the practical question is what the system does during one: refuse or block (CP, like ZooKeeper, etcd, or Spanner within its guarantees) or serve possibly stale data and reconcile later (AP, like Dynamo-style stores and DNS).

PACELC adds the everyday trade-off: Else (normal operation), Latency versus Consistency, because strong consistency needs coordination round trips. DynamoDB and Cassandra are typically PA/EL, while Spanner and other consensus-based databases are PC/EC. Many systems are tunable per request (Cassandra consistency levels, DynamoDB strongly consistent reads), so the honest interview answer names the choice per operation: payments CP, like counts AP.

Linearizability makes the system behave like a single copy with real-time ordering; it is needed for locks, leader election and uniqueness checks, and costs coordination latency. Sequential consistency keeps one global order but not real time. Causal consistency preserves cause-and-effect order (a reply never appears before its post) and is the strongest model that stays available during partitions. Session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads) are cheap and fix most user-visible anomalies.

Eventual consistency only promises convergence once writes stop; in practice convergence is usually fast but has no hard bound, so design for the anomalies: show a pending state, make operations commutative, or reconcile in the background. Do not confuse this with the C in ACID, which is about constraints. Interviewers probe whether you can name the weakest model that is still correct for a given feature.
swe-system-design-04.further: Study consensus (Raft is the most approachable), linearizability versus serializability, and how distributed SQL databases provide strong consistency across regions. Kleppmann's 'Designing Data-Intensive Applications' chapters on replication, partitioning and consistency are the standard reference, and the Jepsen analyses show how real databases violate their claimed guarantees. Explore CRDTs for collaborative apps, rebalancing strategies in Cassandra and Redis Cluster, change data capture for keeping derived stores in sync, and tunable consistency levels in production databases.

panels:
Queues turn a synchronous chain into asynchronous steps: the producer only needs the broker to be available, not every downstream service, so a slow email provider no longer slows checkout. They also smooth load: a burst of 10,000 orders per second can be absorbed by the queue and drained at whatever rate workers sustain, a pattern called queue-based load leveling.

The costs are real: eventual consistency (the invoice appears a few seconds later), harder debugging across asynchronous hops (propagate trace IDs in message headers), duplicate and out-of-order messages, and another piece of critical infrastructure to operate. Use a queue when the caller does not need the result to answer the user. Keep synchronous calls when the user must see the outcome immediately, such as card authorization, or use a request/reply pattern with a status endpoint the client can poll.

In a work queue (RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS) a message is delivered to one consumer and deleted after it is acknowledged; if the consumer does not acknowledge within a visibility timeout, it is redelivered to someone else. This is ideal for task distribution. In pub/sub each subscriber gets its own copy, which enables fan-out to independent services.

Kafka unifies both with a log: messages are retained for a configured time (days, or forever with compaction) regardless of consumption, every consumer group reads the whole topic independently (pub/sub across groups), and within a group partitions are split among members (queue-like work sharing). Because data is retained, consumers can replay history after a bug fix or bootstrap a new service. Traditional brokers are better at per-message routing, priorities and delayed delivery; log-based systems excel at throughput, ordering per key and replay.

A partition is an ordered, append-only log; each message gets an increasing offset, and a consumer group stores its committed offset per partition. The producer's default partitioner hashes the key, so all events for order_id 123 go to the same partition and are seen in order. Messages without a key are spread across partitions with no ordering guarantee.

Partition count caps parallelism within a group and is hard to change later, because adding partitions changes key-to-partition mapping and breaks per-key ordering for existing keys; plan for future peak throughput. Replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas = 2 and acks = all is the common durability setting. When consumers join or leave, the group rebalances partition assignments; cooperative rebalancing (incremental) avoids stopping the whole group. Very large partition counts increase metadata and recovery cost, although KRaft-based clusters handle far more partitions than older ZooKeeper-based ones.

The guarantee is decided by when you commit relative to doing the work. At-most-once commits first: fast, no duplicates, but a crash loses the message, which is acceptable for metrics sampling. At-least-once processes first: nothing is lost, but crashes, rebalances and producer retries create duplicates. It is the sensible default.

Exactly-once in Kafka means idempotent producers (deduplicated by producer ID and sequence number) plus transactions that atomically write output messages and commit consumer offsets, giving exactly-once for read-process-write pipelines that stay inside Kafka. As soon as a side effect leaves the system (sending an email, calling a payment API, writing to another database), you are back to at-least-once and need idempotency at the destination. The phrase to use in interviews: exactly-once delivery is impossible in general; exactly-once processing is achievable with idempotence or transactions.

An idempotent operation produces the same final state whether it runs once or many times. Some operations are naturally idempotent (set status = shipped, or an upsert keyed by order_id); others are not (increment a balance, send an email) and need deduplication. The pattern shown records the message ID in the same database transaction as the business effect, so either both happen or neither does. In real code, make the seen-table insert fail on a unique constraint rather than relying only on a read check, which closes the race between two concurrent duplicates.

Use a stable ID chosen by the producer (an event ID or business key), not the broker offset, which changes if the message is re-published. Bound the dedup table with a TTL longer than the maximum redelivery window. For external APIs, pass an idempotency key so the provider deduplicates for you.

Retry transient failures (timeouts, 503s) with exponential backoff and jitter; do not retry permanent failures (validation errors) at all. Kafka has no built-in DLQ, so frameworks implement retry topics (orders.retry.1m, orders.retry.10m) and a dead-letter topic; SQS and RabbitMQ support DLQs natively through a maximum receive count or dead-letter exchanges. A DLQ needs an owner, alerting and a redrive tool, or it becomes a silent data graveyard.

Backpressure means the system signals 'slow down' instead of collapsing: bounded buffers, producer throttling or blocking when buffers fill, rate limits at the edge, autoscaling consumers on lag (KEDA in Kubernetes), and shedding low-priority work. Consumer lag (latest offset minus committed offset, or better, the age of the oldest unprocessed message) is the key health metric, because a queue hides failures until its delay becomes user-visible.

Events describe facts in the past tense (OrderPlaced), while commands request actions (ChargeCard). Events let new consumers join without the producer knowing about them, which is the decoupling win, but they make the overall flow implicit and harder to see. Document event schemas in a schema registry (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) with compatibility rules, so producers cannot break consumers by renaming fields.

Decide what goes in the event: thin events (an ID only, consumers call back for details, which reintroduces coupling and load) or fat events (carry the needed state, larger but self-contained). Using order_id as the key keeps all events of one order in sequence for each consumer. Event sourcing goes further, storing the event log itself as the source of truth and deriving current state by replaying it; it is powerful for audit trails but adds complexity with schema evolution and rebuilding projections.

A poison message is retried forever and blocks every later message in its partition, because Kafka consumers process each partition in order. Catch errors per message, retry a bounded number of times, then park the message in a DLQ. Ordering is per partition only; cross-key ordering requires a single partition, which kills parallelism. Retrying via a separate retry topic also reorders messages for that key.

The dual-write problem: committing to the database and then publishing can fail between the two steps, leaving them inconsistent. The transactional outbox pattern writes the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, and a relay (polling, or change data capture such as Debezium) publishes it, giving at-least-once publication. Answer to the check: each partition is assigned to only one consumer in a group, so 4 partitions keep at most 4 consumers busy; the other 6 sit idle.
swe-system-design-05.further: Next, learn the transactional outbox and inbox patterns, change data capture, schema registries and compatibility modes, and Kafka internals (in-sync replicas, log compaction, KRaft). Compare log-based streaming (Kafka, Redpanda, Pulsar) with traditional brokers (RabbitMQ, SQS) and cloud event buses. Stream processing frameworks (Kafka Streams, Flink) add windowing, joins and state on top of logs. Also study workflow engines such as Temporal, which handle retries, timeouts and long-running processes more explicitly than chains of queues.

panels:
The real driver for microservices is organizational: Conway's law says systems mirror the communication structure of the teams that build them, and microservices let dozens of teams deploy independently without coordinating releases. The price is distributed-systems complexity: network failures, eventual consistency, versioned contracts, and much more infrastructure (CI/CD per service, observability, service discovery).

A modular monolith gets many of the benefits with one deployable: enforced module boundaries (separate packages, no reaching into another module's tables, interfaces between modules checked by tooling), in-process calls, and real transactions. It is also the easiest starting point for extracting services later, because the seams already exist. Several well-known companies have publicly moved some microservice systems back to monoliths for cost and simplicity. Interview framing: choose the architecture that matches team size, domain maturity and scaling needs, and explain the migration path rather than declaring a winner.

A bounded context, from domain-driven design (DDD), is a boundary inside which a model and its vocabulary are consistent: 'Customer' in Billing (payment methods, invoices) differs from 'Customer' in Support (tickets, history), and forcing one shared model couples everything. Good service boundaries usually follow business capabilities and contexts, not technical layers; a 'database service' or a 'validation service' is a red flag.

Database-per-service is what makes independent deployment real: other services use the owner's API or its events, never its tables. Data needed elsewhere is copied through events into local read models, which means accepting eventual consistency. Signs of wrong boundaries: chatty calls for every request, features that always touch several services, and lockstep deploys. Start with coarse services and split when a boundary has proven stable; merging services back later is much more painful.

An API gateway handles cross-cutting edge concerns: TLS termination, authentication (validating tokens and passing identity downstream), rate limiting, request routing, protocol translation and sometimes response aggregation. The Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern gives each client type (web, mobile) its own gateway layer tailored to its needs. Keep business logic out of the gateway, or it becomes a new monolith that every team has to change.

Service discovery can be client-side (the client queries a registry and load-balances itself) or server-side (a load balancer or proxy does it). In Kubernetes, a Service gets a stable DNS name and virtual IP, and endpoints update as pods become ready. A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) adds sidecar or node proxies providing mutual TLS between services, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and telemetry without changing application code, at the cost of operational complexity.

Timeouts should be set from the callee's latency distribution (for example a little above its p99.9) and propagate as a deadline: if the user request has 1 s left, downstream calls must not wait 2 s. Retries need exponential backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized retry waves, a cap, and a retry budget (for example retries may add at most 10% extra load). Retry at one layer only: three layers each retrying 3 times multiply into 27 attempts against a struggling service.

A circuit breaker tracks failures over a sliding window; when it opens, calls fail immediately or return a fallback (cached data, a default, a degraded feature) instead of tying up threads. After a cool-down it goes half-open and lets a few trial requests through. Bulkheads add isolation by giving each dependency its own connection pool or thread pool, so one slow dependency cannot exhaust everything else.

Two-phase commit across services is avoided because it blocks while a participant is unavailable and couples every service to a coordinator. A saga splits the business transaction into local transactions, each publishing an event or replying to an orchestrator; if a step fails, compensating transactions semantically undo the earlier steps, for example refunding a charge. Compensation is not a true rollback: emails may already be sent, so design steps in a sensible order, putting the risky or irreversible ones last.

Choreography (services react to each other's events) is decoupled but hard to follow as the number of steps grows; orchestration (a coordinator, often a workflow engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions) makes the flow explicit, testable and observable. Sagas lack isolation, so intermediate states are visible; countermeasures include semantic locks (an order in PENDING state), commutative updates and re-reading values before acting. Every step and compensation must be idempotent.

Microservices make sense when several teams step on each other in one codebase, when parts of the system need very different scaling or reliability, or when isolation is required (a payment component under strict compliance rules). They hurt when the domain is still changing (boundaries will be wrong), when the team is small, or when the platform basics are missing: automated deployment, centralized logs, metrics, distributed tracing and on-call ownership per service.

The strangler fig pattern is the safe migration path: route one capability at a time through a facade to a new service, keep the monolith running for everything else, and retire old code incrementally. Extract the piece with the clearest boundary and the strongest reason first, for example a high-load, independently scaling component. Interviewers like candidates who can say 'not yet' and explain what would change their mind.

A distributed monolith has all the costs of microservices and none of the benefits: services that share a database or libraries containing domain logic, synchronous call chains, and coordinated releases. Availability multiplies across synchronous dependencies: 0.999^5 = about 0.995, which raises expected downtime from roughly 43 minutes to about 3.6 hours per month. Reduce depth with asynchronous messaging, caching and fallbacks.

Retry storms happen when every layer retries a failing service and turns a small outage into a large one; budgets, jitter and circuit breakers contain them. Other common problems: no distributed tracing, which makes debugging guesswork; inconsistent API versioning, which breaks consumers; too-fine services ('nanoservices') with more network overhead than logic; and lack of contract tests, which leaves teams to discover breaking changes in production.
swe-system-design-06.further: Read about domain-driven design (bounded contexts, context mapping, aggregates), the strangler fig migration pattern, and team topologies for aligning services with teams. Study resilience patterns in depth (bulkheads, load shedding, deadline propagation, retry budgets), distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, and consumer-driven contract testing. Workflow engines such as Temporal make sagas easier to build and observe. Sam Newman's 'Building Microservices' and 'Monolith to Microservices' are practical references for when and how to split a system.

panels:
REST models a system as resources identified by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP methods, so caches, proxies and client libraries understand requests without custom knowledge. Use plural nouns, keep nesting shallow (/users/42/orders is fine, deeper chains are not), and model actions that do not fit CRUD as sub-resources (POST /orders/42/cancellation) rather than verbs in paths.

Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) do not change state; idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) have the same effect when repeated, which is what makes automatic retries safe. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent: a JSON Patch 'append' applied twice appends twice. POST creates or triggers actions and is neither safe nor idempotent, which is why it needs idempotency keys. Return 201 with a Location header after creation, and use consistent naming, error formats and timestamp formats (ISO 8601, UTC) across the whole API.

Precise codes let clients react programmatically: 401 means 'authenticate' (the name Unauthorized is historical and misleading), 403 means 'authenticated, but not allowed', 404 can deliberately hide a resource's existence from unauthorized users, 409 signals a state conflict (duplicate, version mismatch), 412 Precondition Failed pairs with If-Match for optimistic concurrency, 422 is common for semantic validation errors, and 429 should carry a Retry-After header.

On the server side, 502 and 504 indicate a bad or slow upstream, and 503 means temporarily unavailable, ideally with Retry-After. Clients should usually retry 429, 503 and 504 with backoff, but not most 4xx responses. Use a structured error body such as RFC 9457 problem details (type, title, status, detail) with a machine-readable code and a request ID for support. Never return 200 for a failure, since monitoring, caches and clients all trust the status code.

GraphQL exposes a typed schema; clients send queries selecting exactly the fields and nested relations they need, which suits varied frontends and avoids both over-fetching and multiple round trips. Trade-offs: everything is a POST to one URL, so HTTP caching needs persisted queries or client caches; naive resolvers cause N+1 database calls (solved with batching via DataLoader); and expensive nested queries need depth limits and cost analysis to prevent abuse. Errors arrive in an 'errors' array, often with HTTP 200.

gRPC defines services in .proto files and generates typed clients and servers in many languages. Protocol Buffers are compact and fast to parse, HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls over one connection, and four call types are supported (unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional). Browsers need gRPC-Web or a proxy, and long-lived HTTP/2 connections need L7, per-request load balancing.

Pick from the consumers outward. Public APIs for third-party developers favor REST with JSON plus OpenAPI documentation, because every language and tool supports it and HTTP caching works out of the box. Product teams with many screens and clients that change quickly often put GraphQL in front of internal services, typically as a gateway or federated graph. Internal service-to-service traffic, especially with high call volumes, strict contracts or streaming, favors gRPC.

Other options worth naming: WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for server push, webhooks for notifying third parties (signed payloads, retries, idempotent receivers), and asynchronous APIs that return 202 Accepted with a status URL for long jobs. Whatever the style, the durable parts of API design are the same: a stable contract, clear errors, pagination, authentication, rate limits and backward-compatible evolution. Mixing styles is normal; switching later costs far more than choosing deliberately.

Prefer additive, backward-compatible evolution: add optional fields and endpoints, never rename or remove fields or change their meaning, and make clients tolerant of unknown fields. When a breaking change is unavoidable, introduce a new major version (/v2 in the path is the most visible; header or media-type versioning keeps URLs stable), run both in parallel, announce deprecation with Deprecation and Sunset headers, and monitor usage of the old version before removing it. Some APIs use date-based versions pinned per client account.

Offset pagination makes the database read and discard offset rows (OFFSET 100000 is slow) and shifts results under concurrent inserts. Cursor (keyset) pagination encodes the last seen sort key, for example (created_at, id), into an opaque token and queries WHERE (created_at, id) < (...) ORDER BY ... LIMIT 20, which is index-friendly and stable. Its trade-off: no jumping straight to page 50 and no cheap total count.

Token bucket: capacity B allows bursts up to B, refill rate r sets the sustained average. Implement it lazily, storing tokens and last_refill per key, and on each request add (now - last_refill) x r, capped at B. In a distributed setup, keep state in Redis and update it atomically with a Lua script, or accept approximate per-node limits.

Alternatives: leaky bucket (smooths output to a constant rate), fixed window counters (simple but allow double bursts at window boundaries), sliding window log (exact but memory-hungry) and sliding window counter (a good approximation). Communicate limits with headers such as RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After. Choose the key carefully (API key, user, IP address, or tenant) and apply different limits per endpoint cost. Rate limiting protects fairness and capacity; for overload protection add load shedding and concurrency limits too.

Idempotency keys make non-idempotent POSTs safe to retry over unreliable networks. The client generates a unique key (a UUID) per logical operation and reuses it on every retry. The server atomically records the key with a 'processing' state before doing work, then stores the final status code and body; retries return the stored response. A concurrent duplicate that arrives while the first is still processing gets 409 or waits.

Store a hash of the request body with the key and reject reuse with different parameters (often 422). Keep keys for a bounded window, for example 24 hours, longer than any client retry policy. Scope keys per account to prevent collisions or probing. Payment APIs popularized the Idempotency-Key header, and an IETF draft standardizes it. Remember that this only covers the HTTP layer: downstream side effects still need their own idempotency.

Verbs in URLs duplicate what HTTP methods already express and lead to inconsistent APIs; use resources and methods instead. Returning 200 with an error body breaks retries, monitoring and caches. Unbounded list endpoints work in testing and then time out in production: always paginate, with a default and maximum page size. Breaking changes without versioning silently break mobile apps that cannot be force-updated, and old app versions live for years.

Other frequent mistakes: leaking internal database IDs or schemas, inconsistent naming (camelCase mixed with snake_case), timestamps without a timezone, missing authentication on 'internal' endpoints, and chatty APIs that need ten calls to render one screen. Answer to the check: offset counts rows from the top, so when a new item is inserted at the top, every item shifts down one position, and the next page starts one row too early, repeating an item, or one too late, skipping one when items are deleted.
swe-system-design-07.further: Learn OpenAPI for describing and generating REST APIs, RFC 9457 problem details for errors, HTTP caching with ETags and conditional requests, and authentication flows (OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, API keys, mutual TLS). Explore GraphQL federation, gRPC deadlines and streaming, and webhook design with signatures and retries. For rate limiting, study distributed algorithms and the IETF RateLimit headers. API style guides published by large platforms are excellent references for naming, pagination and versioning conventions.

panels:
Requirements turn an ambiguous prompt into a scoped problem, and interviewers grade whether you ask the right questions. Functional: who are the users, which core features (and which are explicitly out of scope, such as user accounts or link editing), and do links expire? Non-functional: scale (writes and reads per day), read-to-write ratio, latency targets, availability (99.9% versus 99.99%), durability (a link must never break), consistency (must a new link work instantly worldwide?), and security (abuse, malware links, guessable codes).

Write the agreed list on the board and refer back to it; every later decision should trace to a requirement. Prioritize: the redirect path is the product, so its latency and availability matter far more than link creation. If the interviewer says 'you decide', state a reasonable assumption out loud and move on rather than stalling. Five minutes is a guide; spend less if the scope is obvious.

Show the arithmetic: 100M / (30 x 86,400 s) is about 39 writes/s; at 100:1 reads that is about 3,900 reads/s, and a 2-3x peak factor gives around 10,000 reads/s. Storage: 100M x 12 months x 5 years = 6B records; at about 500 bytes each (long URL averaging a few hundred bytes plus metadata), that is 3 TB before replication, so about 9 TB with 3 replicas. That fits a modest sharded cluster.

Cache sizing: if 20% of daily-active links serve most traffic, a cache of tens of GB covers the hot set and fits in a few Redis nodes. Bandwidth is tiny: 10,000 redirects/s x about 500 B = 5 MB/s. Code space: 62^6 is about 57 billion and 62^7 about 3.5 trillion; 7 characters gives headroom and makes random guessing hits rare. Conclude by saying what the numbers imply: reads dominate, so optimize the read path.

Keep the API minimal and explicit. POST /v1/urls takes long_url plus optional custom_alias and expires_at, returns 201 with the code and short URL, and should accept an Idempotency-Key so a retried request does not create duplicates. Validate URLs (scheme allow-list, length limits) and scan them for malware or phishing, since shorteners are a favorite tool of abusers. Add per-user and per-IP rate limits.

The redirect status is a real design choice. 301 (permanent) is cached by browsers, so repeat clicks never reach you: lower load, but you lose analytics and cannot change or disable the target. 302 or 307 (temporary) brings every click back, enabling counting, expiry and takedowns. Most commercial shorteners use 301 or 302 depending on product needs. Expired or unknown codes return 404 or 410 Gone. Optional extras: GET /v1/urls/{code}/stats and DELETE for owners.

The access pattern is overwhelmingly point lookups by code, with no joins on the hot path, which suits a key-value or wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) or a sharded relational database. Relational still works fine at about 40 writes per second and gives an easy unique constraint for custom aliases; the main pressure is storage size and read volume, which caching absorbs.

Shard by hash(code) for an even spread; sharding by user_id would make the hot redirect lookup scatter across all shards. If 'list my links' is needed, add a secondary table or index keyed by user_id, accepting that it is updated asynchronously or written to both. Store created_at and expires_at for expiry and cleanup, and consider a separate click-events store (a columnar or time-series database) so analytics writes never compete with redirect reads. Replicate each shard 3x across zones for durability.

Walk through both paths. Create: API server -> get a unique ID -> base62-encode it -> write to the database -> return the short URL. Redirect: API server -> Redis lookup -> on a miss, read the database and fill the cache -> 302 -> asynchronously publish a click event to a queue. The redirect path never waits on analytics.

Code generation options: (1) a counter plus base62 gives unique, compact codes without collision checks, but needs a distributed ID source and produces guessable sequences; (2) random 7-character codes are unguessable but need a uniqueness check, which stays cheap while the space is sparse (6B of 3.5T is under 0.2% full); (3) hashing the long URL (MD5 truncated) deduplicates identical URLs but collisions must still be handled. A CDN or edge cache in front can serve the most popular redirects close to users.

Interviewers choose one or two areas to probe, so offer options and ask which they prefer. ID allocation: a coordination service (or a database sequence) hands each server a block such as 1,000 IDs at a time; a crash wastes at most one block, which is harmless. Alternatives are Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) with no coordination per ID.

Caching: an LRU Redis cluster with TTLs; precompute nothing, since the cache fills itself on demand; protect against stampedes on viral links with request coalescing. Custom aliases share the same namespace, so enforce uniqueness with a conditional insert and reserve words like 'api' and 'admin'. Expiry: check expires_at on read (lazy), and run a background job to delete expired rows and invalidate cache entries. Analytics: aggregate click events in a stream processor into per-minute counts, rather than updating counters in the main database on every click.

Name the bottleneck, the fix, and the cost. Database read load: caching plus read replicas; writes are low, so sharding is mainly for storage. Single points of failure: multiple API instances across zones, a replicated cache, a highly available ID allocator. Hot links: edge caching and in-memory caches on API servers. Guessable codes: shuffle sequential IDs with a reversible permutation (for example, multiply by a large number coprime to 62^7, modulo 62^7, or a small block cipher) so codes look random but stay unique.

Also discuss consistency: a new link must be readable immediately by its creator (read from the primary, or write through to the cache), while analytics can be minutes behind. Multi-region: replicate links globally (they are immutable, which makes replication easy) and serve redirects from the nearest region. Close by summarizing which requirements each choice serves and what you would monitor (p99 redirect latency, cache hit ratio, error rates).

Common failure modes in interviews: jumping into a favorite technology before understanding the problem; designing in silence; never quantifying, so you cannot justify sharding or caching; ignoring failures (what happens when the cache, a zone or the ID service goes down?); over-engineering for scale the requirements never mentioned; and getting lost in one component while the end-to-end flow is still missing.

Good signals: structured progress, explicit assumptions, numbers that drive decisions, trade-offs stated as 'X gives A at the cost of B', and responsiveness to hints. For the check: 1B new URLs per month is about 385 writes/s, around 38,500 reads/s at 100:1 with peaks near 100,000/s, and 60B URLs in 5 years at 500 B is about 30 TB before replication. Codes: 62^7 (about 3.5 trillion) still suffices, but sharding is now clearly required.
swe-system-design-08.further: Practice the framework on other classics: rate limiter, news feed, chat system, web crawler, notification service, distributed key-value store and ride matching. Each emphasizes a different deep dive (fan-out, connection handling, politeness, consistency). Study ID generation schemes (Snowflake, UUIDv7, ticket servers), Bloom filters, and probabilistic counting such as HyperLogLog for unique-visitor analytics. Rehearse aloud with a timer, and review real architecture write-ups from engineering blogs to see how the trade-offs played out in production.
